## Overview

The Lenca are an Indigenous people from present-day southwest Honduras and eastern El Salvador in Central America. In Honduras, they are the largest Indigenous group, with an estimated population of more than 450,000. Lenca communities are associated with the Comayagua Valley, the departments of Intibucá, La Paz, Lempira, and Santa Bárbara, and areas around Lake Yojoa, the Jicatuyo River, and the Pacific lowlands of Honduras. Before European contact, Lenca settlements also occupied El Salvador, including Quelepa and Chalchuapa. The Lencan languages form a small language family. Historically, the people spoke several dialects, including Chilanga, Putun or Potón, and Kotik, but most Lenca people today are native speakers of Spanish. Their folk culture is documented through pottery, agricultural customs, communal ceremonies, foodways, archaeology, and continuing efforts to preserve or recover the Lenca language.

## Material culture

### Textile & pattern traditions

**Motif vocabulary.** The sources name no Lenca textile motifs.

### Clothing & dress

They state that commoner Lencas historically paid tribute in honey and cotton cloaks. The sources also mention cotton among the crops cultivated by Lenca communities and identify cotton cloaks in the historical social order.

### Architecture

Lenca towns were found in valleys or, occasionally, on fortified crags. They were comparatively small and were mainly constructed from adobe rather than stone. In the Comayagua Valley, prehistoric Lenca settlements were typically located along major rivers, providing access to water for drinking and washing and to waterways for transportation. The Lenca built relatively few and small monumental public structures, except for military fortifications.

Archaeological sites associated with Lenca settlement include Yarumela, Los Naranjos, Quelepa, Tenampúa, and Chalchuapa. Yarumela was a primary Lenca center during the middle and late formative periods. Los Naranjos and Chalchuapa were each dominated by a constructed earthen mound. Other sites had large, open, flat plazas, leveled by manual grading, and dominated by massive two- to three-tiered pyramidal earthwork mounds. Tenampúa was protected by a series of walls that remained visible when the site was described.

### Ceramics, metalwork & everyday objects

Lenca pottery is the best-documented material expression of Lenca identity in the sources. During the Pre-European Era, Lencan pottery was similar to pottery made by other Mesoamerican groups, especially Maya groups and several groups from central Mexico. Modern Lencan pottery is described as distinctive and is handcrafted by Lenca women. Custom pottery continues to be made in the town of Gracias, Honduras, and surrounding villages, especially La Campa.

The pieces are usually dark orange or brick-colored, and visitors can watch demonstrations of their manufacture. In the mid-1980s, cooperatives of women artisans were created to market pottery. Their designs and styles were encouraged to respond to urban buyers and foreign markets. In the 21st century, Lenca women also made modern painted pottery, often painted black and white, that was not based on traditional designs. Archaeological ceramics include Usulua Polychrome and Usulután-style ceramics, which connected Lenca settlements with neighboring chiefdoms during the classic period.

## Music & performance

They do document performance within the annual Guancasco ceremony. Guancasco is held by neighboring communities, usually two, to establish reciprocal obligations and confirm peace and friendship. Processions, elaborate exchanges of greetings, and folk dancing are performed for the statue of the patron saint of the town.

The ceremony takes many forms and includes Catholic representations as well as traditional customs and representations. Towns in central and western Honduras, including Yamaranguila, La Campa, and La Paz, host annual celebrations, as do towns in eastern El Salvador south of Honduras, including Lolotique, Yucuaiquin, and Guatajiagua.

Lenca men also participate in ceremonies connected with the cultivation and harvest of crops. During different crop seasons, they consume chicha and burn incense. No UNESCO Intangible Cultural Heritage inscription concerns the Lenca in the supplied material.

## Dance & theatre

The principal named performance tradition in the sources is folk dancing during Guancasco. Neighboring communities gather annually, process, exchange greetings, and perform folk dances for the statue of the town’s patron saint. Guancasco has both Catholic representations and traditional customs and representations.

## Festivals & rituals

Guancasco is an annual ceremony in which neighboring communities, usually two, gather to establish reciprocal obligations and confirm peace and friendship. Its forms vary, and it includes processions, exchanges of greetings, folk dancing, Catholic representations, and traditional customs. The performance is carried out for the statue of the patron saint of the town. Annual Guancasco celebrations are documented in Yamaranguila, La Campa, La Paz, Lolotique, Yucuaiquin, and Guatajiagua.

The Lenca also maintain ceremonies associated with crop cultivation and harvest. During different crop seasons, Lenca men consume chicha and burn incense. Earlier Lenca lordships agreed to truces at certain times of the year; these agreements are remembered by the Lencas as the *wankasku*, or Guancasco, ceremony. They state that the original religion was polytheistic, included elements of nahualism, and had a strong connection to the environment. Contemporary Lenca practice is primarily Roman Catholic, adopted during the colonial Spanish era, while some communities retain more exclusively Indigenous customs.

## Foodways

Historically, commoner Lencas cultivated cornfields and grew roots and crops including yuca, potato, sweet potato, cacao, beans, squash, chiles, and cotton. Their agricultural production was supplemented by hunting deer, armadillo, agouti, paca, wild turkey, duck, and macaw. In the modern milpa crop-growing system, Lenca communities cultivate coffee, cacao, tobacco, varieties of plantains, gourds, maize, wheat, beans, squash, sugarcane, and chili peppers. Peanuts are also cultivated in El Salvador.

Traditional foods named in the sources include *Atol Shuko*, described as a black corn paste that looks purple; *Tamales Pisques*; *Miel de Jocote*, or jocote syrup; *Miel De Mango*, or mango syrup; *Panal De Abeja*, or bee hives; *Cuzuco*, identified as armadillo; *Garrobo*, identified as stone iguana; *Chakalines*, identified as river shrimp; and *Punches*, identified as river crab. The sources also state that Lenca men consume chicha during ceremonies associated with crop seasons and burn incense at those times.

Lenca communities traditionally expect all members to participate in communal efforts. Most Lenca people continue to use traditional agricultural practices on their own crops and on crops raised for investors.

## Oral tradition & literature

They do document a continuing interest in language preservation. In the case of Salvadoran Lenca, Consuelo Roque and Mario Salvador Hernández wrote a learning primer titled *Poton piau, nuestra lengua Potón*. In 2017, Alan R. King and James Morrow published *Kotik molka niwamal*, described as a compilation of Lenca words from communities still existing and as opening the possibility of recovering a significant part of the language.

A 2002 novel by Roberto Castillo, *La guerra mortal de los sentidos*, chronicles the adventures of the “Searcher for the Lenca Language.” The sources also mention programs and dictionaries intended to revitalize the Lenca language and culture and rehabilitation projects in El Salvador intended to prevent the extinction of Salvadoran Lenca.

## Language & religion

The Lencan languages are a small language family native to Central America. During the Pre-Columbian era, their speakers lived throughout El Salvador and Honduras. The two attested languages are Salvadoran Lencan and Honduran Lencan. Salvadoran Lencan was spoken in Chilanga and Guatajigua, while Honduran Lencan was spoken with minor dialect differences in Intibucá, Opatoro, Guajiquiro, Similatón, modern Cabañas, and Santa Elena. The sources also name Chilanga, Putun or Potón, and Kotik among historical Lencan varieties.

Honduran Lenca is currently believed to be extinct. Salvadoran Lenca is described as having one remaining speaker in one section of the source, while another section states that no one is known to speak Lenca fluently and that some individuals retain fragments or partial knowledge. Most Lenca people today are native speakers of Spanish.

The original religion was polytheistic, incorporated elements of nahualism, and maintained a strong connection to the environment. Contemporary Lenca people primarily practice Roman Catholicism, adopted during the colonial Spanish era, often by force. Some communities combine Catholic practice with pre-European customs, including ceremonies connected to cultivation and harvest in which men consume chicha and burn incense.
